title: Preventive care: who is screened for what, and when

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on current USPSTF recommendations. Ages and intervals change with each update; review before trusting.

questions.q: From what age does colorectal cancer screening begin for average-risk adults?
questions.why: Through 75, then selectively to 85. Colonoscopy every ten years or an annual faecal immunochemical test are the commonest choices; any positive stool test needs a colonoscopy.

questions.q: Screening mammography is recommended every two years from what age for average-risk women?
questions.why: Through 74 under the 2024 recommendation, which lowered the start from 50. Dense breasts and family history prompt a conversation about supplemental imaging or earlier risk assessment.

questions.q: How is cervical cancer screening done between ages 30 and 65?
questions.a: HPV testing every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years
questions.why: From 21 to 29 it is cytology alone every three years. Screening stops at 65 with adequate prior negative results, or after a hysterectomy for benign disease.

questions.q: Who qualifies for annual low-dose CT screening for lung cancer?
a: Currently smoking or quit within the past 15 years
d: Anyone with a family history of lung cancer
Anyone with COPD regardless of smoking
questions.why: All three criteria together. Screening stops once the person has not smoked for 15 years or develops a condition that limits life expectancy or the ability to have surgery.

questions.q: Who gets a one-time abdominal ultrasound to screen for aortic aneurysm?
questions.a: Men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked
d: Women over 65 who have ever smoked
questions.why: Men in that age range who have never smoked may be offered it selectively. There is insufficient evidence for women, even smokers.

questions.q: Prostate-specific antigen screening is a shared decision for men in which age range?
questions.why: It is not recommended at 70 or older. The conversation covers the small mortality benefit against overdiagnosis and the harms of treatment.

questions.q: Screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes is recommended for overweight or obese adults from what age?
questions.why: Through 70, repeated every three years if normal. A fasting glucose, an A1c, or an oral glucose tolerance test all serve.

questions.q: Which infections should every adult be screened for at least once regardless of risk?
questions.why: Hepatitis B, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and tuberculosis are screened by risk. Pregnancy triggers its own panel.

questions.q: What does the guidance say about starting low-dose aspirin for primary prevention at age 60 or older?
d: Start it if blood pressure is controlled
Start it if cholesterol is high
questions.why: For ages 40 to 59 with a ten-year risk of 10% or more it is an individual decision, and the net benefit is small. Bleeding risk rises with age faster than the benefit does.

questions.q: Which intervention is recommended to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults over 65 at increased risk?
questions.a: Exercise, particularly balance and strength training
questions.why: Vitamin D is no longer recommended for fall prevention in this group. A multifactorial assessment of vision, drugs, footwear and the home is offered selectively.

questions.q: Which conditions should be screened for in all adults, not only those with symptoms?
d: Coronary artery disease with an ECG
questions.why: Anxiety screening is recommended up to 64, and obesity is measured at every visit. Routine thyroid, vitamin D and resting ECG screening in asymptomatic adults are not recommended.

questions.q: What does the guidance say about whole-body skin examination to screen for skin cancer in adults without symptoms?
questions.a: The evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against it
d: Recommended against because it causes harm
questions.why: People with a changing lesion, many atypical moles, a personal or family history of melanoma, or heavy sun exposure are evaluated on clinical grounds rather than as screening.
